Getting started

Source: vignettes/getting-started.Rmd
getting-started.Rmd
library(fabricatr)

fabricatr makes data you do not have yet. You describe the variables and how they relate, and fabricate() builds a data frame that looks like what you expect to collect, so a design can be run and diagnosed before there is anything to analyze.

One level

fabricate() builds a data frame one column at a time. N is the number of rows, and every column can use the columns before it:

survey <- fabricate(
  N = 100,
  age = round(runif(N, 18, 80)),
  income = 20 + 0.5 * age + rnorm(N, sd = 10)
)
head(survey)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 3
#>   ID      age income
#>   <chr> <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1 001      23   21.9
#> 2 002      47   58.8
#> 3 003      61   48.4
#> 4 004      68   52.2
#> 5 005      53   52.2
#> 6 006      73   73.5

fabricate() adds a unit identifier as the first column, named ID unless you choose another name with ID_label. IDs are character strings, zero-padded to the width of the largest one, so these run "001" to "100" and a frame of six rows runs "1" to "6". N = 100 sets the number of rows, and the name N can then be used inside any column’s expression, which is why runif(N, 18, 80) and rnorm(N, sd = 10) each draw exactly one value per row.

Two levels

Real data have structure: citizens in villages, students in schools, years within countries. Each level is a named argument to fabricate(). add_level() builds the first one, here five villages, each with its own village_wealth. nest_level() then builds four citizens inside each village, twenty rows in all. Every citizen row carries the village_wealth of the village it belongs to, so the expression for income can use it:

nested <- fabricate(
  villages = add_level(N = 5, village_wealth = rnorm(N)),
  citizens = nest_level(N = 4, income = village_wealth + rnorm(N))
)
head(nested)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 4
#>   villages village_wealth citizens  income
#>   <chr>             <dbl> <chr>      <dbl>
#> 1 1                 0.192 01        0.0316
#> 2 1                 0.192 02        0.311 
#> 3 1                 0.192 03        0.810 
#> 4 1                 0.192 04       -0.848 
#> 5 2                 1.30  05        2.55  
#> 6 2                 1.30  06        1.62

N inside a level means the number of rows that level is building. In nest_level(N = 4, ...) you supply 4 per village, but the expressions inside see N as 20, so rnorm(N) gives each of the twenty citizens a draw of their own. Each level names its own ID column after itself, here villages and citizens, in place of ID.

Potential outcomes

An experiment has an outcome under treatment and an outcome under control, and observes only one of them. potential_outcomes() writes both down from a formula, one column per condition. Z in the formula is not a column: it names the treatment, and the formula is evaluated once with Z = 0 and once with Z = 1, giving Y_Z_0 and Y_Z_1:

experiment <- fabricate(
  N = 100,
  U = rnorm(N),
  potential_outcomes(Y ~ 0.5 * Z + U)
)
head(experiment)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 4
#>   ID        U Y_Z_0 Y_Z_1
#>   <chr> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 001   0.702 0.702 1.20 
#> 2 002   0.152 0.152 0.652
#> 3 003   1.83  1.83  2.33 
#> 4 004   2.03  2.03  2.53 
#> 5 005   1.30  1.30  1.80 
#> 6 006   0.821 0.821 1.32

Once units are assigned, reveal_outcomes() picks out the outcome each unit shows. A call that starts from data takes N from it, so N here is nrow(experiment), 100:

observed <- fabricate(
  data = experiment,
  Z = rbinom(N, 1, 0.5),
  Y = reveal_outcomes(Y ~ Z)
)
head(observed)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 6
#>   ID        U Y_Z_0 Y_Z_1     Z     Y
#>   <chr> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <int> <dbl>
#> 1 001   0.702 0.702 1.20      1 1.20 
#> 2 002   0.152 0.152 0.652     1 0.652
#> 3 003   1.83  1.83  2.33      1 2.33 
#> 4 004   2.03  2.03  2.53      0 2.03 
#> 5 005   1.30  1.30  1.80      0 1.30 
#> 6 006   0.821 0.821 1.32      0 0.821

Draws that look like real variables

The draw_* family turns a latent variable into the kind of measurement a survey produces. draw_binary() gives a 0/1 outcome. latent is the variable on the scale the link works on, so with link = "logit" each unit is a 1 with probability plogis(x):

fabricate(
  N = 6,
  x = rnorm(N),
  voted = draw_binary(latent = x, link = "logit")
)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 3
#>   ID          x voted
#>   <chr>   <dbl> <int>
#> 1 1     -3.35       0
#> 2 2     -1.06       0
#> 3 3     -0.0204     0
#> 4 4      0.576      1
#> 5 5     -0.286      1
#> 6 6     -0.0579     1

draw_normal_icc() draws a clustered variable with a target intra-cluster correlation, so that citizens in the same village resemble each other by the amount you choose:

clustered <- fabricate(
  villages = add_level(N = 100),
  citizens = nest_level(N = 20, trust = draw_normal_icc(clusters = villages, ICC = 0.3))
)
icc_share <- summary(lm(trust ~ villages, data = clustered))$adj.r.squared
icc_share
#> [1] 0.2495772

The adjusted figure is the one to read: it is the share of variance lying between villages, which is what the ICC sets. The ICC is a parameter of the draw rather than a property of any one data set, so the realized share varies around it, with a standard deviation of about 0.03 across draws of a hundred villages. This draw lands at 0.25. Plain r.squared runs about 0.03 higher still, because it counts the ninety-nine village dummies as explanatory power.

draw_normal_ar() is the same idea over time. declare_level() builds a level that does not nest in the one before it: here 2,000 units and, separately, 6 periods. cross_levels() then pairs every unit with every period, giving a panel of 12,000 rows, one per unit per period, and .by names the two levels being crossed. The draw then gives each unit a series whose shocks persist, so a unit resembles its own recent past by the amount rho sets:

panel <- fabricate(
  units = declare_level(N = 2000),
  periods = declare_level(N = 6),
  obs = cross_levels(
    .by = c("units", "periods"),
    shock = draw_normal_ar(clusters = units, time = periods, rho = 0.7)
  )
)
head(panel)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 4
#>   units periods obs    shock
#>   <chr> <chr>   <chr>  <dbl>
#> 1 0001  1       00001 -0.306
#> 2 0002  1       00002 -1.38 
#> 3 0003  1       00003 -2.37 
#> 4 0004  1       00004  0.657
#> 5 0005  1       00005  0.596
#> 6 0006  1       00006  0.202

To see the persistence, put each period in its own column, one row per unit, and correlate the first period with the rest:

wide <- tapply(panel$shock, list(panel$units, panel$periods), sum)
round(cor(wide)[1, ], 2)
#>    1    2    3    4    5    6 
#> 1.00 0.71 0.50 0.36 0.25 0.15

The correlation with the first period falls as the gap grows. In expectation it is 0.7 one period later, 0.49 (0.7 squared) two periods later, and in general 0.7 raised to the gap; a sample of 2,000 units lands within a couple of hundredths of each.

Resampling

resample_data() bootstraps a data frame, and respects its levels: villages are drawn with replacement, then citizens within each village that was drawn. A village can come up more than once, and its citizens are resampled separately each time.

boot <- resample_data(nested, N = c(villages = 3, citizens = 2))
boot
#> # A tibble: 6 × 4
#>   villages village_wealth citizens  income
#>   <chr>             <dbl> <chr>      <dbl>
#> 1 1                 0.192 02        0.311 
#> 2 1                 0.192 03        0.810 
#> 3 3                -0.559 11       -1.11  
#> 4 3                -0.559 12        0.0117
#> 5 1                 0.192 04       -0.848 
#> 6 1                 0.192 01        0.0316

ALL in place of a number keeps every unit at that level, and leaving a level out of the plan does the same thing:

resample_data(nested, N = c(villages = 3, citizens = ALL))
#> # A tibble: 12 × 4
#>    villages village_wealth citizens income
#>    <chr>             <dbl> <chr>     <dbl>
#>  1 4                -0.513 13       -1.23 
#>  2 4                -0.513 14        0.380
#>  3 4                -0.513 15       -1.40 
#>  4 4                -0.513 16       -1.00 
#>  5 5                 2.42  17        3.29 
#>  6 5                 2.42  18        2.13 
#>  7 5                 2.42  19        1.63 
#>  8 5                 2.42  20        2.87 
#>  9 2                 1.30  05        2.55 
#> 10 2                 1.30  06        1.62 
#> 11 2                 1.30  07        1.74 
#> 12 2                 1.30  08        1.88

Where to read next

The book at https://book.declaredesign.org puts fabricated data to work in complete research designs, and vignette("fabricatr2.0") lists what changed from fabricatr 1.x for anyone with an older script. Every function is documented in the reference index.
